vignette:
Amina is a 35-year-old African American woman who works as a private tutor, spending most afternoons in family homes and after-school programs with elementary-aged children. She describes her life as split into a before and after, though when she tries to explain what happened, her words often fail her. The assault occurred after an evening tutoring session when she accepted a ride from a man she knew casually through the neighborhood. What remains most vivid to her is not a coherent story but fragments: the sudden shift from ordinary conversation to danger, the sickening awareness that she had lost control of what was happening, and the terror that flooded her body when she realized she could not stop him. When she reaches this part in session, she goes quiet and looks away. She says the memory does not feel like it is hers, “like it happened to some other woman,” yet at the same time any contact with it brings back the same raw terror she felt that night.

In the weeks afterward, Amina found herself caught between feeling detached from the event and being overwhelmed by it. If she let her mind drift anywhere near it, she became certain she would not be able to handle what came up. She began to treat her own thoughts as dangerous. She would interrupt them, turn on the television, scroll on her phone, or leave the room if someone’s conversation seemed to be moving toward sexual violence or even general discussion of women’s safety. When other people referred to rape in the news or in casual conversation, she felt cornered, as if the room had suddenly narrowed around her. She stopped attending gatherings where she might be exposed to unexpected reminders, and when her partner gently tried to ask what she was going through, she would shut down or say she was tired. It seemed safer to keep distance than to risk being pulled back into something she felt she could neither describe nor survive.

Her work makes some of her triggers impossible to avoid. Amina tutors children one-to-one, and crying is part of the landscape of her job: a frustrated second grader in tears over homework, a younger sibling wailing in the next room, a child melting down after school. The sound hits her body before she can think. She feels a wave of nausea, her stomach tightening so sharply that she sometimes has to excuse herself to the bathroom. In those moments she is no longer simply in a client’s home or at a tutoring table; she is gripped by the same terror she remembers from the assault, even if she cannot fully narrate why. She has become wary of situations that feel unpredictable. A schedule change, a parent running late, an unfamiliar route to a student’s house, even not knowing who else will be in the home can leave her tense and scanning. Uncertainty itself has come to feel dangerous.

Over time, her life has narrowed. She has turned down potentially enjoyable invitations from her partner and friends because feeling happy or hopeful now seems risky and somehow wrong. She has come to believe that she has permanently changed for the worse, that whatever version of herself used to feel open, confident, and capable is gone. Alongside this is a relentless habit of blaming herself. She goes over small decisions from that night again and again, as if enough scrutiny might produce a different ending: why she accepted the ride, what she said, what she failed to notice, what she should have done. The repetition does not bring clarity, but she continues because it feels intolerable to leave the questions unanswered.

She also speaks as though her resilience has been stripped away. Minor upsets that once would have passed—a child becoming upset during a lesson, a misunderstanding with her partner, a day of disrupted plans—now feel to her like proof that she cannot cope with anything. This belief has begun to affect her work. She has limited the number of families she sees, avoids assignments in unfamiliar neighborhoods, and sometimes cancels at the last minute when she wakes feeling nauseated and afraid of what the day might hold. Her partner has noticed that she seems absent even when physically present, and that she pulls away whenever life begins to feel warm or promising.

Amina came for help after leaving a tutoring session abruptly when a child started crying loudly over a reading exercise. She locked herself in the client’s bathroom, shaking and nauseated, and afterward sat in her car with the conviction that she was no longer fit to do the job she loves. What frightened her most was not only the intensity of that moment but the sense that she is becoming someone fragile and permanently damaged, someone who cannot bear either distress or hope. At the same time, beneath the fear, she wants relief from living as if danger is waiting in every uncertain moment, and she wants, cautiously, to believe that what happened can belong to her story without destroying her.
